blocks.text: *Küştdepdi* is a Turkmen rite of singing and dancing. UNESCO describes it as a performing art built on improvised poetry about good feelings and good wishes: singers make up their verses as they go, and dancers answer the tune with their hands, their gestures and their feet. In December 2017 it was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Its home is the west of the country. Turkmenistan's inventory of its heritage places it mainly in seven districts of Balkan province, on the coast of the Caspian Sea, among them Esenguly, Hazar and Türkmenbaşy, and to a lesser extent in parts of the other four provinces. There it belongs to family celebrations, an engagement, a wedding, the birth of a child, and to national holidays and festivals.

**How it is danced.** According to the inventory, the rite opens with respected women, seated, singing their best wishes in verse. Then a pair of singers, traditionally a woman and a man, lead the song, and the dancers move in a half-closed or closed circle around them. The dance starts from the right foot with one, two or three steps, then a stamp and a clap. No instrument is needed: the clapping of the listeners and the voice of the male singer keep the rhythm, and the circle speeds up as the singers warm to it.

**What it is for.** The words are wishes, the same kind you learned in this unit: for happiness, health, peace and plenty, and for the young couple at a wedding. The inventory says the rite was also meant to keep misfortune and the evil eye away from the family. The name itself is not explained in the UNESCO file. One account, published on the websites of Turkmenistan's embassies, calls it a bird's dance and links it to the fishermen of the Caspian coast and their trips out to sea; it is told as a story, not as a fact of record.

**Who keeps it.** Masters of the song and the dance, women and men, teach it to younger performers, mostly by doing it together. When it was nominated, more than fifteen folklore groups with over 350 performers were active, and music schools and cultural centres teach it too. At a wedding, though, nobody needs a school: everyone joins the circle.

blocks.title: Words for the circle
blocks.text: *aýdym* is a song and *aýdymçy* a singer; *tans* is a dance, *tans etmek* to dance. A good wish is a *ýagşy dileg*. And at a wedding, the wish everyone says to the hosts: *Toýuňyz gutly bolsun!*
With this unit's wishes and **let's**, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Küştdepdi gadymy aýdym we tans. Ony köplenç toýda aýdýarlar. Iki aýdymçy ortada aýdym aýdýar, beýlekiler tans edýärler. Aýdymda ýagşy dilegler köp: “Toýuňyz gutly bolsun! Ýaşlar bagtly bolsun!” Geliň, biz hem tans edeliň!
blocks.en: Küştdepdi is an old song and dance. It is often sung at weddings. Two singers sing in the middle, and the others dance. There are many good wishes in the song: “Congratulations on your celebration! May the young couple be happy!” Come on, let's dance too!

questions.q: Where is küştdepdi mainly at home?
options: on the Caspian coast, in Balkan province
questions.explain: Turkmenistan's inventory names seven districts of Balkan province, on the Caspian coast, among them Esenguly and Hazar.

questions.q: What keeps the rhythm of the dance?
options: the clapping and the singer's voice
questions.explain: No instrument is needed: the listeners clap and the male singer's voice sets the beat.

questions.q: In the reading, what is in the song?
questions.explain: *Aýdymda ýagşy dilegler köp*: there are many good wishes in the song.
